newsitem.title: USA: Bank reform schedule in House Commerce not yet set.
newsitem.headline: Bank reform schedule in House Commerce not yet set.

text.p: The House Commerce Committee is still working on a schedule for considering sweeping legislation to overhaul U.S. financial laws, one of the committee's subcommittee chairman said on Tuesday.
Rep Michael Oxley, chairman of the finance and hazardous waste subcommittee, said the committee would hold at least one hearing in July with top regulators.

"We would have one hearing with the superstars, hopefully the week we're back from the (July) recess and everything else is fairly fluid at this point," the Ohio Republican told reporters after a hearing on the legislation in Washington.

The reform legislation, narrowly approved by the House Banking Committee on Friday, would allow banks, insurance companies and securities firms to combine and also would allow commercial companies to own small banks.
The Commerce Committee historically has jurisdiction over insurance matters and will receive the reform bill under a sequential referral from the Banking Committee.
Oxley deferred comment on the substance of the bill as approved by the Banking Committee. "We're still picking through the entrails and that will take a while," Oxley said.
Under a typical sequential referral, the committee would have to act within 30 days of formally receiving the legislation from the Banking Committee.
Some members of the Commerce Committee want more time and could put off consideration until after Congress returns from the August recess, congressional staffers said.

Even if the Commerce Committee approves the bill, the legislation's fate remains murky. The Senate has not acted on a companion bill and strong opposition among industry groups has blocked earlier reform efforts several times in the past decade.
Earlier on Tuesday, Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley said the reform effort needed a "rebalancing" in regards to state insurance regulation of bank insurance sales.

The bill would allow federal bank regulators to overrule state insurance regulations in some instances. Insurance companies have complained that the provision will lead to unfair and less-stringent regulation of bank insurance sales.

"It is an unfortunate result of the different systems of regulation that the playing field is so imbalanced," Bliley, Republican of Virginia, said in a statement. "Fortunately, it is a balance that Congress can correct.
